To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pathogenicity of Rhodococcus is dependent on long‐chain mycotic acids.
the pathogenic bacterium R. equii arrests phagolysosomal maturation in macro phages by means of trehalose dimycolate, a glycolipid that contains long‐chain my colic acid molecules.

(i) the long‐chain fatty acids of mycobacteria are required for phagosome maturing, (ii) the short‐chain fatty acids are unable to divert phagosome maturning, and (iii) this difference is due to the length of the fatty acid chains.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of pathogen‐macrophage interaction and the development of novel strategies for the control of infectious disease.
the molecular mechanisms by which pathogenic R. equisurvives in the host cell.
the role of trehalose dimylcolate and its biosynthesis in the pathogenicity of R. Equi.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the long chain mycolic acid trehalose‐dimycolate is the key molecule responsible for the inhibition of phagolysosomal fusion.
the longer mycolic acids produced by R.  equi play an essential role in the diversion of phagosome matulation.
the long‐chain length of trehalose dimycloate is essential for the ability of R.  equi to divert phagolysosomal maturation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

long‐chain trehalose dimyclocates are required for phagosome trafficking and that the mycolic acid‐synthesizing enzyme responsible is KasA, which catalyses the first committed step of mycolic acids synthesis.
R. equis uses its long‐chain mycocerosates and trehalose dimycocerosates to divert phagosome maturing macrophages into a non‐degradative pathway.
long‐chain trehalose dimycloate is the main virulence factor for R. equis.

the length of mycolic acids is a major factor in the ability of R.  equi to divert trafficking of its phagosome.
